extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and researchers seeking an encyclopedic summary of the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear accident
extracted.subtask_description: A comprehensive Wikipedia encyclopedia entry describing the causes, sequence, technical failures, consequences, and aftermath of the 2011 Fukushima Daiichi nuclear accident. Covers reactor design, emergency systems, evacuation and health effects, radionuclide releases, and policy effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: International Nuclear Event Scale classification
rubrics_metrics.description: International Nuclear Event Scale Level 7 (major accident).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article states the accident is regarded by the United Nations Scientific Committee on the Effects of Atomic Radiation as the worst nuclear incident since Chernobyl and records UN commentary that 'no adverse health effects among Fukushima residents have been documented that are directly attributable to radiation exposure from the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear plant accident'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolation condenser (IC) design and required capability
rubrics_metrics.description: Each reactor was initially designed to be equipped with two redundant isolation condensers (ICs) each capable of cooling the reactor for at least 8 hours (at which point the condenser tank would have to be refilled).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IC involved a closed coolant loop with a heat exchanger; because the IC could cool too rapidly after shutdown (causing thermal stress), protocol called for operators to manually open and close the condenser loop using electrically operated control valves. Loss of DC/AC control can render ICs inoperable or cause isolation valves to close automatically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reactor Core Isolation Cooling (RCIC) system specification
rubrics_metrics.description: RCIC systems (introduced after Unit 1) used reactor steam to drive a turbine powering a pump to inject water and were designed to operate for at least 4 hours (until depletion of coolant or mechanical failure); they could be converted to a closed-loop system drawing coolant from the suppression chamber.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RCIC could function autonomously without an external energy source (besides reactor steam), but required DC to remotely control it and AC to power isolation valves. RCIC operation and ability to be reconfigured (recirculate from suppression chamber) were central to cooling in the accident.

rubrics_metrics.name: On-site backup power and Emergency Diesel Generators (EDG) redundancy and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Two EDGs were available for each of units 1–5 and three for unit 6 (13 EDGs total). Ten of the 13 EDGs were water-cooled and placed in basements ~7–8 m below ground; the other three were air-cooled and sited elsewhere. Switchable interconnections allowed reactors to share EDGs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The placement of water-cooled EDGs and associated seawater pumps on the shoreline made them vulnerable to tsunami flooding. The vulnerability and placement choices contributed to the loss of AC power after the tsunami.

rubrics_metrics.name: Backup DC battery capability and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Backup DC batteries were designed to be kept charged by AC power and to be able to power the station for approximately 8 hours without EDGs. Their physical placement varied by unit (basements for units 1,2,4; turbine building raised above ground for units 3,5,6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Loss of AC power and subsequent loss of DC in certain units (1,2,4) impaired remote control and monitoring and contributed to failure modes such as automatic valve closures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seismic design tolerances and earthquake resistance standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Original design basis: zero-point ground acceleration of 250 Gal and static acceleration of 470 Gal; after 1978 Miyagi earthquake standards required reactors to withstand accelerations up to 450 Gal (re-evaluated in 2006).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 9.0 MW earthquake produced maximum ground g-forces of 560, 520, and 560 Gal at units 2, 3, and 5 respectively, exceeding the seismic reactor design tolerances of those units and contributing to the station blackout and damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venting protocol for preventing overpressure/explosion
rubrics_metrics.description: In an emergency, operators planned to vent steam manually by venting valves to prevent a high-pressure explosion; steam released would be expected to be not very radioactive if fuel remained in primary containment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Venting involved lowering reactor/PCV pressure to allow low-pressure injection of water; lack of power and pneumatic/valve failures complicated venting (rupture disks, isolation valves, need for compressors), and delayed venting contributed to containment and core damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency water injection and use of firefighting equipment
rubrics_metrics.description: When designed cooling systems failed, operators planned to inject water into reactors using fire protection equipment, diesel-driven fire pumps, or fire trucks; seawater injection was used when freshwater supplies were depleted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In many instances DDFPs were inoperable or inaccessible, injection ports were hidden under debris, seawater injection lines were damaged by explosions, and reinstitution of seawater injection required repairs and improvisation (mobile generators, external pump lines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spent fuel pool cooling and monitoring requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Spent fuel pools required cooling; during the accident temperatures rose (e.g., to 61 °C at the common spent fuel pool on 21 March) and water spraying and restoration of dedicated cooling systems were used to reduce temperatures (power restored to cooling systems 24 March; temperatures down to 35 °C by 28 March).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitoring pool temperature and maintaining water inventory are essential; inspections (aerial, crewed) and concrete pump/spraying were used when standard systems were unavailable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radionuclide release quantification and key isotopes
rubrics_metrics.description: Atmospheric release estimates expressed for major products: 137Cs (7–20 PBq), 131I (100–400 PBq), xenon-133 (6,000–12,000 PBq). Direct releases into groundwater/ocean estimated separately (e.g., 1–5.5 PBq 137Cs and 10–20 PBq 131I).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article describes that 40–80% of atmospheric 137Cs was deposited in the ocean; most deposited radionuclides were iodine and caesium; ocean currents (Kuroshio) dispersed contaminants widely. Different measurement programs gave context on environmental impacts and persistence in marine species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evacuation and shelter-in-place orders and their radii
rubrics_metrics.description: Evacuation orders evolved: initial 2 km radius evacuation of 1,900 residents, then near-simultaneous 3 km evacuation (~6,000 residents) and 10 km shelter-in-place for 45,000 residents; evacuation radius later expanded to 10 km then revised to 20 km; a 30 km shelter-in-place order was later communicated, followed by voluntary evacuation recommendations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article highlights that zone sizes were 'set for arbitrary reasons at the discretion of bureaucrats rather than nuclear experts', that communication between authorities was scattered, and that overlapping/changed orders caused multiple relocations, additional harm (e.g., 51 evacuation-attributed deaths among hospital/nursing-home patients), and long-term displacement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Health monitoring, screening, and interpretation standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Large-scale screening programs (including thyroid examinations for children and ongoing epidemiological surveys) reported elevated detection rates for certain conditions; experts attribute much of this increase to enhanced medical surveillance rather than radiation exposure itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surveillance must be interpreted carefully — increases in detected conditions may reflect intensified screening. The article notes that one death had insurance compensation paid for lung cancer but this does not prove causal relationship with radiation; overall, UN committees reported no documented adverse health effects directly attributable to radiation exposure among residents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigative findings on preparedness: risk assessment and evacuation planning standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigations faulted lapses in safety and oversight, namely failures in risk assessment and evacuation planning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report-level criticism implies that acceptable preparedness should include robust risk assessments accounting for tsunamis, properly sited and protected backup systems (EDGs, batteries), clear evacuation plans and communication protocols, and record-keeping of key meetings during crises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication and public information handling standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The Japanese public perceived the government and TEPCO as providing limited information in the early weeks; expert analysis understandable to laypersons was delivered by a retired reactor designer rather than official sources. SPEEDI data distribution and delays in sharing mapping information were criticized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective crisis communication requires timely release of understandable expert analysis, forwarding critical monitoring data to relevant agencies and external partners, and avoiding suppression of key terms (e.g., instructions not to use 'core meltdown' delayed acknowledgment). Failures in records and data forwarding were documented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental and oceanic impact assessment standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorities and institutes (e.g., French Institute for Radiological Protection and Nuclear Safety) characterized the release as the most important individual oceanic emissions of artificial radioactivity observed; assessments consider ocean currents, deposition patterns, and persistence in marine life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations should measure atmospheric and direct oceanic releases, track dispersion (currents), monitor seawater and sediments, and interpret consequences for marine life; the article notes that coastal contamination may persist due to continued runoff from contaminated soil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychosocial and evacuation-related health impact criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Mental health and evacuation side effects included stress, depression, anxiety, sleep disturbance, PTSD, maternal distress, increased substance use and obesity (children recommended to stay indoors); surveys reported deteriorated health and family separation for many evacuees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Response evaluations should account for non-radiological harms of evacuation (months of life lost, increased mortality among vulnerable institutionalized populations, long-term psychosocial consequences) and include mental health support as part of disaster response planning.
